doc.title: Wendell Harrison interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 10, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Rhythm changes, blues forms, rock and roll and church music
summary: Harrison describes the original R&B as rhythm changes and 12-bar blues, and how church and popular music share forms.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Yes. Were rhythm & blues creeping into things that people wanted to hear at that time?

No this was like rhythm & blues — do you know the original rhythm & blues is? The original R & B was rhythm changes. Like “I Got Rhythm?” And you had about a thousand tunes that was written basically on that format. You know it’s modified from one tune to the next but basically that, “I Got Rhythm” and it’s like a 32-bar form. Okay. There were so many tunes back in the 30s and 40s that was based on that 32-bar form, with different variations, different variations you know, different keys and then sometimes the jazz musicians would introduce substitution changes and whatnot, because they was trying to deal with their sound, more of a modern progressive sound. And so that was like the rhythm format, and then you had the blues format which is a 12-bar format. And you had a thousand, a million —
You could play the blues all night.

Yeah well there’s so many different kinds of blues, we have blues with bridges you have blues that’s got 12-bar blues and sometimes they would extend it to like playing 12 bars and then play a 4-bar interlude. You know you had all different kinds of — but that was the popular sound of that particular time. And then at the same time there was rock & roll. Frankie Valli, let’s see, Chuck Berry —
Little Richard, okay, Little Richard. But it was still the 12-bar blues.

Still the 12-bar blues. And sometimes, like Ray Charles, sometimes the 12-bar blues would be extended to 16 bars you know, and then you would hear, if you played for church you would hear the same format in churches playing the same formal changes. In fact the church, in the Baptist church, they usually adapt to the music or sound that’s popular and then put spiritual words on top of that. You know if you have a big popular tune that’s in the psyche of everybody they would actually put, somebody would construct a tune which is similar chord-wise and put lyrics, spiritual lyrics on top of it. And it would really serve the purpose of church. Everybody felt good — “Oh that really sounds good.” And they would really go out and buy church music. But they were buying

the same music, you know it’s the same format. So the original R & B, rhythm & blues, was like popular music, 40s and 50s, and I mean the popular music not only blues stuff like Little Richard, but I’m talking about Cole Porter, Rogers & Hart, Gershwin. Those were the major composers at that particular time. And we took those tunes and dressed them up, instead of doing swing we’d play bossa nova, we’d play Latin, we’d play shuffle and change the beat.
